paragraphs: This paper studies the distribution of node representations produced by polynomial graph neural networks in semi-supervised classification. Its theoretical setting assumes a graph with community structure whose average degree grows without bound. Within that setting, the authors establish a central limit theorem describing how representations fluctuate around their centers as the graph becomes large.

The result identifies a stable mixture of multivariate Gaussian distributions after centering and applying a depth-dependent scaling. A related result describes normalized representations together with their labels: their community-associated means stabilize, while their covariance matrices shrink inversely with average degree. The authors explicitly calculate these limiting means and covariances, giving a quantitative account of both location and variability.

As network depth increases, the mixture moves toward a one-dimensional form. This characterizes oversmoothing through the geometry of the representation distribution. The paper also proves that cross-entropy training on these embeddings becomes asymptotically equivalent to training on the nearly collapsed Gaussian mixtures, connecting the distributional analysis to the learning objective.
neurips-2025-a-clt-for-polynomial-gnns-o.tldr: Under a growing-degree community graph model, polynomial GNN embeddings approach Gaussian mixtures whose collapse with depth precisely characterizes oversmoothing.

paragraphs: Removing entire layers can shrink a language model, but it often damages performance. This paper attributes most of that degradation to a mismatch in activation magnitudes where the remaining layers meet. The values arriving at this interface have different scales from those expected downstream, and the resulting distribution shift propagates through the rest of the model.

LinearPatch repairs this interface with two operations combined into one matrix multiplication. A Hadamard transformation suppresses unusually large values associated with particular tokens, while channel-wise scaling aligns activation statistics. The intervention therefore targets the flow of representations at the pruning boundary, providing a lightweight addition to an already pruned model.

On LLaMA-3-8B with five of its 32 layers removed, the method retains up to 94.15% of original performance, with a reported 4% advantage over the previous state of the art. Optional offline distillation using 5,000 unlabeled samples raises retention to 95.16% in 30 minutes on one GPU. These findings support activation-scale repair as a substantial recovery mechanism in the evaluated setting.
neurips-2025-a-simple-linear-patch-reviv.tldr: LinearPatch recovers much of a layer-pruned language model’s performance by correcting activation scales at the pruning interface.

paragraphs: Spiking neural networks often represent information through firing rates. Obtaining precise outputs with this coding scheme can require many time steps, increasing latency and energy costs. The problem is especially relevant when conventional artificial neural networks are converted into spiking networks. Adaptive Fission addresses the encoding of an already trained network to reduce this dependence on long computation periods.

The method selectively splits highly sensitive neurons into groups with different scales and weights. These groups provide neuron-specific precision and threshold allocation, concentrating additional representational capacity where it is needed. The authors describe this as a generalized form of population coding, with minimal additional spatial overhead.

Because the modification happens after training, it applies to a range of pretrained spiking architectures without further training or fine-tuning. Experiments on neuromorphic hardware report reductions of up to 80% in latency and power consumption without an accuracy decrease. The findings show that selectively changing how neurons encode information can substantially improve the measured efficiency of pretrained spiking models.
neurips-2025-adaptive-fission-post-train.tldr: Adaptive Fission selectively splits sensitive spiking neurons after training, achieving up to 80% reductions in latency and power consumption without degrading accuracy.

paragraphs: Language-model agents can gather and interpret information about users and items while deciding what to recommend. Evaluating these systems requires accounting for their interactions with an environment, including how they respond when user interests change or information is scarce. AgentRecBench addresses the lack of a shared evaluation setup for this emerging approach to personalization.

The paper introduces an interactive text-based simulator containing detailed user and item metadata. It covers conventional recommendation, evolving interests, and cold-start tasks. A unified modular framework also supports building agentic recommenders, allowing their components to be studied within a common environment. Together, these resources connect system development with evaluation across distinct recommendation conditions.

The benchmark compares more than ten classical and agentic methods. The authors report superior performance from agentic systems in their evaluation and derive practical guidance for designing their core components. They also report validating the environment through an open challenge. The contribution is both comparative evidence and shared infrastructure for studying adaptive recommendation behavior.
neurips-2025-agentrecbench-benchmarking-.tldr: AgentRecBench provides a shared simulator, development framework, and benchmark for evaluating language-model agents as personalized recommenders.

paragraphs: The paper studies sequences whose observations are independent and identically distributed once a shared latent factor is given. Autoregressive models can represent uncertainty in these settings by generating missing observations. The authors ask which inference procedures and Transformer architectures make that representation useful for decisions such as active learning and bandit problems.

They identify a fundamental weakness in single-step generation: it cannot distinguish uncertainty about what is known from randomness inherent in the observations. Multi-step autoregressive generation supports this distinction. The paper demonstrates better uncertainty quantification with multi-step inference and shows that these improvements translate into better downstream decision-making performance.

The architectural analysis reaches a separate cautionary conclusion. Several specialized Transformer designs intended for exchangeable sequences cannot guarantee exchangeability, despite their additional computational overhead. Empirically, these designs can perform substantially worse than standard causal masking. Together, the findings favor careful attention to the inference procedure and show that architectural specialization alone does not ensure the desired probabilistic behavior.
neurips-2025-architectural-and-inferenti.tldr: Multi-step generation improves uncertainty-based decisions, while several specialized Transformer architectures fail to guarantee exchangeability and can underperform standard causal masking.

paragraphs: Diffusion Transformers become expensive at high image resolutions because their attention computations grow quadratically with the number of tokens. CLEAR investigates how to replace this attention in pretrained models while retaining generation quality. The authors identify four useful design factors: locality, consistency with the original formulation, high-rank attention maps, and preservation of feature information.

Their attention mechanism restricts each query token to a surrounding local window, producing linear computational complexity. Knowledge is transferred from a pretrained teacher by fine-tuning the student’s attention layer on 10,000 self-generated samples for 10,000 iterations. The experiments report generation results comparable to those of the teacher after this adaptation.

For 8K-resolution image generation, CLEAR reduces attention computation by 99.5% and accelerates overall generation by a factor of 6.3. These are distinct measurements: the reduction in one component produces a smaller end-to-end speedup. The paper also investigates zero-shot transfer across models and plugins, along with improved support for inference distributed across multiple GPUs.
neurips-2025-clear-conv-like-linearizati.tldr: CLEAR adapts pretrained diffusion Transformers to local, linear-complexity attention, reporting comparable quality and 6.3-times faster generation at 8K resolution.

paragraphs: Two videos can resemble each other in one respect and differ in another. Matching actions do not necessarily imply matching locations, so a single overall similarity score can conceal meaningful distinctions. This paper introduces Concept-based Video Similarity estimation, or ConViS, to make the basis of a comparison explicit.

ConViS assigns similarity scores to a video pair across a predefined collection of semantic concepts. The accompanying ConViS-Bench dataset contains annotated pairs from multiple domains, with concept-specific scores and written descriptions of similarities and differences. This structure supports interpretable comparisons and applications such as retrieving videos according to a particular concept specified by the user.

The authors evaluate several leading models and examine how closely their judgments match human annotations. Results show substantial performance differences and reveal that some concepts are more difficult to compare than others. The benchmark therefore makes it possible to study specific strengths and weaknesses that broad similarity scores can obscure, while providing a common task for language-guided video understanding.
neurips-2025-convis-bench-estimating-vid.tldr: ConViS-Bench evaluates whether models can compare videos along explicit semantic concepts and match human judgments of their similarities and differences.

paragraphs: Pretrained Stable Diffusion models contain useful information about sharp images, but guiding them with a blurry input creates a structural challenge. Using a separately deblurred image can instead make the result heavily dependent on that preliminary network. DeblurDiff develops an adaptive guidance mechanism inside the latent representation used by the diffusion process.

The method jointly trains a Latent Kernel Prediction Network with conditional diffusion. This network predicts spatially varying kernels that process blurry features through element-wise adaptive convolution. Different locations can therefore receive different restoration operations while preserving information from the input. The processed latent features guide Stable Diffusion toward sharper structure and more detailed reconstruction.

Guidance is refined throughout generation: the result of each diffusion step helps estimate the kernels used at the next step. This couples kernel prediction with the evolving restoration instead of fixing the guidance at the beginning. Experiments report better deblurring than the compared state-of-the-art methods on benchmark and real-world images, supporting the effectiveness of this iterative latent-space approach.
neurips-2025-deblurdiff-real-word-image-.tldr: DeblurDiff repeatedly predicts spatially adaptive latent-space filters to guide diffusion-based deblurring while preserving information from the blurry input.

paragraphs: Eye-movement prediction often reduces recorded gaze to fixation points linked by rapid movements. That simplification discards information in the continuous trajectory. Models that output a single scanpath of predetermined length also struggle to represent the variation between people viewing the same image. DiffEye learns from raw eye-tracking trajectories to generate continuous, diverse gaze behavior.

Its diffusion model is conditioned on the natural image being viewed. A component called Corresponding Positional Embedding connects gaze locations with semantic features from image patches. This gives the generator a way to relate where the eyes move to the content at those locations, while learning the variability present in recorded trajectories.

The authors report realistic trajectory generation despite using a comparatively small training dataset, alongside state-of-the-art scanpath generation results. Generated trajectories can also be transformed into scanpaths or saliency maps. The contribution therefore extends the output being modeled while retaining compatibility with established summaries of visual attention, which the authors report better reflect its human distribution.
neurips-2025-diffeye-diffusion-based-con.tldr: DiffEye uses image-conditioned diffusion to generate continuous, varied eye-movement trajectories from raw gaze recordings.

paragraphs: Zero-shot out-of-distribution detection asks whether an image belongs outside the categories a system expects, without training a detector on that task. Vision-language models can do this by comparing images with textual class labels. DualCnst adds visual reference information to approaches that primarily expand the set of candidate labels in text.

The framework generates synthetic images for both expected classes and mined out-of-distribution labels using a text-to-image model. Each test image receives a combined score based on its semantic match to labels and its visual match to these synthesized examples. This adds a second source of evidence without requiring actual in-distribution images or additional training.

The theoretical analysis shows that incorporating negative labels through multiple modalities reduces score variance and improves separation between expected and unexpected inputs. Experiments across diverse benchmarks report state-of-the-art detection performance. The framework also remains compatible with earlier text-only methods, making the visual consistency signal a complementary component that can strengthen an existing label-based detection approach.
neurips-2025-dualcnst-enhancing-zero-sho.tldr: DualCnst combines text-label similarity with similarity to generated reference images to improve zero-shot out-of-distribution detection.

paragraphs: Long prompts increase language-model computation and can also reduce performance. This paper studies whether parts of the model itself can identify which input tokens are most useful before full inference. The authors find particular attention heads, called evaluator heads, that can select important information from long inputs.

Their method, EHPC, uses these heads in the first few Transformer layers during prompt processing. The model effectively skims the input, selects significant tokens, and passes the resulting shorter prompt onward for inference. This compression procedure requires no training, and its efficiency comes from using a limited initial computation to reduce the amount of text processed afterward.

EHPC achieves reported state-of-the-art results on benchmarks for prompt compression and long-context acceleration. It also improves performance while reducing commercial API costs compared with other prompt compression methods. Comparisons with key-value cache acceleration show competitive results. Together, the findings suggest that early attention heads can provide useful token selection signals for reducing the cost of long-context tasks.
neurips-2025-efficient-prompt-compressio.tldr: EHPC uses selected attention heads in early Transformer layers to compress long prompts without training and improve inference efficiency.

paragraphs: Dataset distillation creates a small synthetic training set intended to retain the usefulness of a much larger dataset. This paper finds that the process does not automatically reduce unfairness toward minority groups. In the authors’ investigation, compression typically worsens that bias, making the treatment of protected attributes such as gender and race an explicit design concern.

FairDD changes how synthetic data are matched to the original dataset. It simultaneously matches groups defined by protected attributes, addressing the majority dominance that can arise when matching the overall distribution. This encourages synthetic examples to represent all groups and counteracts their collapse toward the majority. The framework works with multiple matching-based distillation approaches without changing their original architectures.

Theoretical analysis and experiments report substantial fairness improvements over conventional distillation, with a promising balance between fairness and target-task accuracy. Consistent gains across distribution and gradient matching support the framework’s versatility. The central finding is that group-aware matching can improve whose information survives dataset compression while preserving useful classification performance.
neurips-2025-fairdd-fair-dataset-distill.tldr: FairDD improves fairness in distilled datasets by matching synthetic data to protected-attribute groups simultaneously.

paragraphs: Vision-language models can understand many aspects of images yet still struggle with spatial relationships in complex three-dimensional scenes. This paper investigates improving those abilities through spatially informative image data. Its approach uses scenes with known three-dimensional structure to generate and annotate two-dimensional training examples.

The resulting pipeline creates tasks ranging from basic spatial perception to more involved reasoning. The authors use it to build SPAR-7M from thousands of scenes across multiple public datasets. They also introduce SPAR-Bench, which evaluates spatial capabilities with both single-view and multi-view inputs. This pairs a training resource with an evaluation setup designed to cover spatial understanding more comprehensively.

Models trained on SPAR-7M together with large-scale two-dimensional datasets achieve state-of-the-art results on two-dimensional spatial benchmarks. Additional fine-tuning on datasets for specific three-dimensional tasks yields competitive results. These findings support the value of supervision derived from three-dimensional ground truth for teaching spatial reasoning through image inputs, with the reported three-dimensional task results involving further task-specific training.
neurips-2025-from-flatland-to-space-teac.tldr: SPAR-7M uses image tasks grounded in known 3D scenes to improve vision-language models’ spatial perception and reasoning.

paragraphs: This paper develops a randomized way to construct binary neural networks with tunable accuracy. Inspired by hyperdimensional computing, it represents data as high-dimensional binary vectors and compares them using Hamming distance, which measures differing bits. The construction treats binary representation as a geometric embedding problem rather than relying on ordinary numerical quantization.

The authors first define floating-point G-Nets, a network family flexible enough to mimic standard layers. Each has a randomized binary counterpart called an embedded hyperdimensional G-Net. Concentration-of-measure arguments provide theoretical guarantees for retaining the floating-point model’s accuracy through this embedding. This establishes an explicit mathematical connection between the original network and its binary representation.

Empirically, the binary models match convolutional neural network accuracies and substantially outperform earlier hyperdimensional computing models. The paper reports almost 30% higher CIFAR-10 accuracy than prior HDC models. These results support randomized embedding as a promising construction route for accurate binary networks, combining an analytical foundation with demonstrated predictive performance.
neurips-2025-g-net-a-provably-easy-const.tldr: G-Net constructs accurate binary networks through randomized high-dimensional embeddings backed by theoretical accuracy guarantees.

paragraphs: Selecting pretraining examples individually can miss how their value depends on relationships with other training data. Group-MATES models those relationships to improve the tradeoff between language-model training cost and downstream quality. It approximates expensive group-level selection using a learned relational data influence model.

To train that model, the authors sample language-model training trajectories and collect oracle influence measurements. The model combines individual influence with relationship-based weights to estimate group influence. For efficient selection, those same relationships partition the dataset into small clusters, within which examples are selected independently. This makes relational selection manageable without treating the entire dataset as one selection problem.

Across the evaluated DCLM configurations and 22 downstream tasks, Group-MATES improves performance by 3.5%–9.4% relative to random selection. Its improvements are nearly twice those achieved by leading individual-selection baselines. It also reduces the tokens needed to reach a given downstream performance by up to a factor of 1.75. Further analyses support both the relationship weights and cluster-based selection.
neurips-2025-group-level-data-selection-.tldr: Group-MATES selects pretraining data using relationships between examples, improving downstream quality and reducing the tokens needed for a target performance.

paragraphs: A video world model must respond to actions while keeping the depicted environment coherent over time. This paper adds action conditioning and autoregressive generation to image-to-video models, then examines why long sequences lose consistency. It identifies compounding prediction errors and insufficient memory as central challenges for interactive world modeling.

The authors report that compounding error is inherently irreducible in autoregressive video generation, while inadequate memory contributes to incoherent worlds. Their proposed video retrieval augmented generation method, VRAG, incorporates explicit global-state conditioning. This gives generation a representation of the broader world state and significantly reduces long-term error accumulation while improving spatial and temporal consistency.

The study also finds that simply extending context windows or applying naive retrieval augmentation is less effective, which it attributes primarily to current video models’ limited in-context learning abilities. The distinction matters because additional history alone does not ensure useful memory. The paper contributes a benchmark alongside its method, providing a setting for evaluating progress toward interactive generation with stronger internal world modeling.
neurips-2025-learning-world-models-for-i.tldr: VRAG uses explicit global-state conditioning to reduce long-term errors and improve coherence in action-conditioned video world models.

paragraphs: Neural B-frame compression predicts a frame using references in both temporal directions. Hierarchical coding can place those references far apart, making continuous motion prediction harder and leaving the two references unevenly useful. BRHVC addresses how a compressor combines this bidirectional information, aiming to extract better motion and contextual guidance from both sides.

The method introduces two components. Bi-directional Motion Converge combines multiple optical flows during motion compression to improve motion compensation over larger scales. Bi-directional Contextual Fusion then assigns weights to reference contexts using the accuracy of that compensation. The weighting explicitly accounts for how well each reference helps predict the current content.

By improving motion estimation and adapting contextual contributions, BRHVC harmonizes the information supplied by its two references. Experiments report better compression performance than previous state-of-the-art neural methods and results exceeding VTM in its random-access configuration on HEVC datasets. These findings support reference coordination as an effective way to improve neural B-frame compression in the evaluated settings.
neurips-2025-neural-b-frame-video-compre.tldr: BRHVC improves neural B-frame compression by combining motion estimates and weighting bidirectional reference information according to prediction accuracy.

paragraphs: Equivariant graph neural networks incorporate symmetry into physical simulation, but the paper argues that existing methods overlook changes in the distribution of dynamics over time. Standard normalization approaches to such non-stationarity can disrupt the symmetry assumptions. NS-EGNN is designed to address changing temporal behavior while preserving the model’s symmetric structure.

The method applies Fourier transforms to trajectory segments to extract frequency information that varies over time. It also uses first- and second-order differences to mitigate non-stationarity, followed by pooling for future prediction. Together, these operations capture changing frequency characteristics and alleviate linear and quadratic trends in the original dynamics.

This combination connects symmetry-aware modeling with explicit treatment of temporal variation. The authors apply NS-EGNN to molecular, motion, and protein dynamics, reporting consistently better performance than existing state-of-the-art algorithms across their evaluated scenarios. The findings support modeling both physical symmetries and changes over time as complementary ingredients for improving the prediction of physical trajectories.
neurips-2025-non-stationary-equivariant-.tldr: NS-EGNN combines symmetry-preserving graph modeling with frequency analysis and temporal differences to predict non-stationary physical dynamics.

paragraphs: Step-by-step language-model reasoning can contain invalid or unsupported inferences. Formal verification offers one route to checking correctness, but producing formal solutions and even formalizing an informal problem remain difficult. This paper instead studies what it means to learn a reliable verifier for sequential reasoning expressed in natural language.

The intended verifier receives a problem and its proposed solution, accepting only when all reasoning steps are valid. The authors place this learning problem in a formal PAC-learning framework, which supports statements about learnability and the amount of data needed. They define several verification objectives with different strengths, allowing reliability requirements to be analyzed separately.

For some objectives, the paper derives upper bounds on sample complexity, establishing sufficient amounts of training data within its framework. For other natural objectives, it proves lower bounds or impossibility results without additional assumptions. The contribution therefore clarifies both achievable verification guarantees and obstacles to stronger ones, providing a theoretical basis for evaluating claims about learned reasoning checkers.
neurips-2025-on-learning-verifiers-and-i.tldr: The paper formalizes learning natural-language reasoning verifiers and proves sample-complexity guarantees alongside limits on stronger verification goals.

paragraphs: Language models can assist evolutionary search by producing candidate algorithms, but the search takes place in an abstract language space. This makes established evolutionary strategies harder to apply directly. The paper develops a general framework that uses features to construct niches within that space, organizing candidates into regions that support niche-based search.

PartEvo builds on this framework by combining collaboration between niches with specialized prompting strategies. Partitioning the search provides structure for exploring algorithm candidates, while collaborative search connects those regions. The aim is to improve the efficiency of automated algorithm discovery by making techniques from evolutionary computation usable in language-model-assisted search.

Experiments on synthetic and real-world optimization problems report better performance than human-designed baselines and earlier language-model evolutionary methods, including Eoh and Funsearch. On resource scheduling, generated meta-heuristics achieve up to 90.1% performance improvement over widely used baselines, with low design costs. These results demonstrate the approach’s potential in the tested optimization settings, particularly for discovering scheduling heuristics.
neurips-2025-partition-to-evolve-niching.tldr: PartEvo organizes language-model-assisted evolutionary search into collaborating niches to improve automated algorithm discovery.

paragraphs: CodeV-R1 trains language models to generate Verilog hardware descriptions from natural-language requirements using reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards. The framework addresses three connected obstacles: obtaining dependable automated verification, building good specification–code pairs, and controlling the computational cost of reinforcement learning.

A rule-based testbench generator checks candidate behavior against reference implementations. For dataset construction, open-source Verilog is described in natural language and then regenerated as code; examples that fail the resulting consistency check are removed. Training begins with reasoning distillation, followed by adaptive DAPO, a reinforcement-learning algorithm that adjusts sampling rates to reduce training cost.

The resulting CodeV-R1-7B model achieves pass@1 scores of 68.6% on VerilogEval v2 and 72.9% on RTLLM v1.1, measuring success on the first generated attempt. The authors report a 12%–20% improvement over prior state-of-the-art results and performance above the 671-billion-parameter DeepSeek-R1 on RTLLM. The findings show how verified data construction and staged training can strengthen hardware-code generation within the evaluated tasks.
neurips-2025-qimeng-codev-r1-reasoning-e.tldr: CodeV-R1 combines testbench-based verification, filtered synthetic data, and staged reinforcement learning to improve Verilog generation.

paragraphs: Single-cell experiments measure different molecular modalities, but combining unpaired measurements is difficult. Existing integration approaches may depend on known correspondences or on a global matrix coupling pairs of observations, restricting flexibility and scale. scMRDR introduces a generative framework for integrating unpaired multi-omics data through structured latent representations.

A beta-variational autoencoder separates each cell’s representation into information shared across modalities and information specific to its modality. Three objectives support this separation: isometric regularization preserves biological variation within each omics dataset, adversarial training encourages alignment across modalities, and masked reconstruction handles features missing across modalities. These components aim to reconcile shared structure without erasing meaningful differences.

Benchmark results show strong performance in batch correction, modality alignment, and preservation of biological signals. The framework also scales to large datasets and supports more than two omics. Its contribution is a combination of representational separation and complementary training objectives that makes integration more flexible while retaining information useful for downstream biological analysis.
neurips-2025-scmrdr-a-scalable-and-flexi.tldr: scMRDR integrates unpaired single-cell modalities by separating shared and modality-specific information while preserving biological variation.

paragraphs: Multi-view clustering groups examples described through several representations or sources. This paper identifies differences in sparsity across views as a cause of inconsistent encodings. Those inconsistencies vary between samples, making a single dynamic weight for an entire view inappropriate for addressing the resulting semantic differences.

SparseMVC tackles this through three modules. An adaptive sparse autoencoder measures each view’s sparsity and adjusts its encoding using an entropy-matching objective. An attention-based module then weights samples by examining relationships between early-fused global features and individual-view features. Finally, a late-fusion module aligns feature distributions across views and supports datasets with an arbitrary number of views.

The design addresses representation mismatch before fusion, balances contributions at the sample level, and aligns distributions afterward. Extensive experiments report state-of-the-art clustering performance. The paper’s central contribution is to treat differing sparsity across views as a distinct modeling problem and connect that diagnosis to adaptive encoding and more finely targeted weighting.
neurips-2025-sparsemvc-probing-cross-vie.tldr: SparseMVC improves multi-view clustering by adapting to differences in sparsity and balancing view contributions separately for individual samples.

paragraphs: Input saliency methods estimate which prompt tokens influence a language model’s output. This paper introduces a stress test inspired by needle-in-a-haystack tasks to assess whether those estimates identify relevant information. Across seven popular methods, the authors find meaningful importance assigned to irrelevant context, with attribution errors growing as prompts become longer.

The proposed Attention Bias Optimization method changes how token influence is measured. It explicitly optimizes the attention bias associated with each input token to quantify its causal impact on generating a target token. This makes attention-bias adjustment the basis of the attribution procedure and directly connects the score to the generation being examined.

Across diverse needle-in-a-haystack tasks, ABO improves reported saliency accuracy by 10%–30% over existing methods and remains effective for prompts up to 10,000 tokens. The paper also demonstrates applications in zero-shot detoxification, sentiment steering, and reasoning-error correction. Its findings pair evidence of attribution failures under long-context stress with a method that improves reliability in those evaluations.
neurips-2025-the-fragile-truth-of-salien.tldr: Attention Bias Optimization improves token attribution after stress tests reveal that existing saliency methods assign importance to irrelevant long-context material.

paragraphs: Prediction with expert advice seeks low cumulative loss relative to the best available expert. This paper considers losses that may be heavy-tailed, assuming only that their second moments are bounded by a quantity called theta. The proposed algorithms adapt without knowing either that bound or the range of losses in advance.

The authors show why a term often treated as secondary in existing regret bounds can become decisive. A term involving the largest loss can scale as the square root of the number of experts times the time horizon, even when theta is a small constant. Consequently, describing that contribution as lower-order can hide a substantial weakness under heavy-tailed losses.

Their algorithms avoid this problematic dependence and guarantee worst-case regret of order sqrt(theta T log K). When losses are independently sampled from a fixed distribution, they obtain order theta log(KT)/Delta_min, where Delta_min separates the best and second-best mean losses. They also improve bounds for squared loss, strengthening guarantees under the paper’s stated moment assumption.
neurips-2025-when-lower-order-terms-domi.tldr: New adaptive expert algorithms improve regret guarantees for heavy-tailed losses by removing a supposedly minor term that can dominate existing bounds.
